title: kc-plan-value v1
description: What to build. Its project block is shaped to lift straight into kc-plan-receipt/v1's project block; every field and bound here is that contract's, not a second opinion about it.

hypothesis.description: Must read 'If we ... then ...'; the shape is the contract. It is a falsifiable claim, so the last milestone's acceptance judges it: say whether the 'then' happened. Written once and never revisited, it is decoration.

wedge.description: The one place to push first, and why it is that one. Name the milestone it became. A wedge that matches no milestone was either not the wedge or was quietly abandoned.

exit.description: What has to be true to call it done. Each entry names the milestone that satisfies it, as 'the milestone: the condition' -- an exit nothing claims is a project that goes green with a condition unmet, and one measured project had three exits and no milestone claiming any of them.

boundaries.description: The shape the code must take, declared once and cited by every technical issue. Not an acceptance criterion: a criterion is one test, a boundary is the constraint that generates them. This is what a peer maintainer reviews a pull request against, and it had no field until a project's was found living as loose prose in a tracker description while its milestone was recut three times without anyone checking the recut against it.

rule.description: Stated so a change can be judged against it, in module and flow terms rather than file paths. 'The reader holds no relay knowledge' survives a refactor; 'move the probe out of that file' was wrong the day it was written.

agreed_with.description: Who agreed, by name or role. A boundary nobody agreed to is a preference.

agreed_at.description: Where the agreement happened and can be read: the pull request, issue or thread. Usually not this tracker, because the other maintainer is usually not in it.

satisfies_exit.description: Which of the project's exit conditions this milestone makes true. The union across milestones has to cover every exit; a gap here is a project that cannot finish and does not say so.

acceptance.description: Something a person does, and for a value issue that is also the proof its parts work together: a value point delivers a person-visible outcome, which cannot be true while any of its technical work is broken. A separate integration-proof field said the same thing in different words on every issue that had one, five out of five.

kind.description: value | defect | measurement. A value issue's assignee owns running its acceptance and recording the result, and owns nothing else -- the building happens in its technical children. Assigning a value issue to whoever builds under it is someone accepting their own work.

independent_because.description: Required when this issue is blocked by nothing: the fact that makes it independent. Silence and 'nobody considered it' are identical in the data; this tells them apart.

assignee.description: Who runs this issue's acceptance, exactly as the tracker spells their name. Required on a value issue: it has no work of its own, so the assignment means one concrete thing. It was prose in a body once, beside the field saying the same name, and the two disagreed within the hour.

user_story.description: 'As <who>, I want <what>, so that <why>.' The first line of the issue, before any heading. A reader who stops there knows what it is for.

dependencies.description: Edges derived from facts, never from the order the stories were told. Each says what must already be true before the blocked issue's acceptance can be run at all.

because.description: The fact, not the narrative. 'X ships before Y in the story' is not a reason; 'Y's acceptance run needs the binary X produces' is.

captain_ruling.description: What the captain saw and ruled before any issue was created. The skill said to draft first and ask; nothing made that fire, and the session that wrote the rule then created two value issues without showing anyone a draft. The projector refuses to create issues without this.

on.description: What was put in front of them: the value points, the milestone, the dependency graph. Name it, so a later reader can tell what was ruled on from what was added afterwards.

changed.description: What the ruling changed. An empty list is a real answer; an absent one means nobody asked.

archaeology.description: What the archaeologist answered before the cut was ruled on. It lived nowhere: the value document had no field for a report, so the captain ruled on evidence the ruled-on artifact could not hold, and the next seat re-excavated it.

changed_the_cut.description: What this answer moved. An answer that changed nothing is worth recording; an answer nobody can trace to a decision is worth asking why it was asked.
